common_name: Spicy Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Fragrant Coral-Orange Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Spicy Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred for exceptional cold hardiness, bears lightly fragrant salmon-orange flowers on a large, vigorous shrub.

directions: Spicy Lights is a University of Minnesota Landscape Arboretum introduction from the cold-hardy Northern Lights azalea breeding program, valued for its ruffled, salmon-orange, funnel-shaped flowers with a light spicy fragrance that open in mid-spring before the leaves fully unfurl. Reaching a substantial 6 to 8 feet at maturity, it is among the larger and most vigorous members of the series and makes a striking specimen or backdrop shrub along a woodland edge. Its flower buds tolerate temperatures well below -30 degrees F, making it one of the few deciduous azaleas reliable in northern gardens where most Southern-bred azalea hybrids fail, and its early flowers are an important nectar source for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. Site in acidic, humus-rich soil with consistent moisture and dappled shade, mulching well to keep roots cool through summer.

common_name: Mandarin Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Fragrant Deep Orange Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mandarin Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred for exceptional cold hardiness, bears vivid reddish-orange flowers reminiscent of Exbury hybrids but far more winter hardy.

directions: Mandarin Lights was bred at the University of Minnesota Landscape Arboretum as part of the cold-hardy Northern Lights series, prized for large trusses of vivid reddish-orange flowers in mid-spring that rival the color of the well-known English Exbury hybrid 'Gibraltar' but with far greater winter hardiness. Growing to 6 or 7 feet with an equal spread, it makes an eye-catching accent at a woodland edge or shaded border where its lightly fragrant blooms draw early-season bumblebees and swallowtail butterflies. Because flower buds are hardy to roughly -35 degrees F, it reliably blooms even after harsh winters that damage the flower buds of less cold-adapted azalea hybrids. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade and mulch to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

common_name: Lemon Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Fragrant Clear Yellow Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Lemon Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred for exceptional cold hardiness, bears clear soft yellow flowers and shows unusually strong mildew resistance.

directions: Lemon Lights is a University of Minnesota Northern Lights series selection bred for extreme cold hardiness, bearing clear, soft yellow, funnel-shaped flowers in generous trusses in mid-spring on a rounded shrub reaching about 4 to 6 feet. It stands out within the series for its notably strong resistance to powdery mildew, a common late-season nuisance on deciduous azalea foliage in humid climates. The pastel yellow flowers brighten a partly shaded woodland planting without the intensity of the series' orange and red-toned selections, and their nectar is readily visited by native bumblebees in early spring. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and avoid heavy clay or poorly drained sites.

common_name: Northern Hi-Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Fragrant Cream-and-Yellow Bicolor Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Northern Hi-Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred for exceptional cold hardiness, bears two-toned creamy yellow-and-white flowers with a bold yellow blotch.

directions: Northern Hi-Lights arose from the same University of Minnesota breeding stock as Golden Lights and is grown for its distinctive two-toned flowers, pale creamy yellow fading to white at the petal margins with a bold yellow blotch on the upper lobe. It is one of the taller Northern Lights selections, reaching 4 to 6 feet, and its large, showy trusses open in mid-spring on bare stems just as the foliage begins to expand. Like the rest of the series, its flower buds withstand temperatures well below -30 degrees F, allowing gardeners in cold climates to grow a fragrant deciduous azalea where more tender hybrids would fail, and its early bloom offers a useful nectar source for emerging native bees. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in dappled shade at a woodland margin, and mulch to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist.

common_name: Orchid Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Fragrant Compact Lavender-Pink Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Orchid Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred from native Rhodora (Rhododendron canadense), bears fragrant lavender-pink flowers on a compact, cold-hardy shrub.

directions: Orchid Lights is a compact University of Minnesota Northern Lights selection derived from a cross of the native Rhodora (Rhododendron canadense) with a cold-hardy Rhododendron x kosteranum hybrid, combining true native genetics with exceptional winter hardiness. Deep purple buds open in mid-spring to fragrant, lavender-pink flowers marked with a darker fuchsia blotch, held on a low, dense, mounding shrub that stays under 4 feet, making it useful for smaller woodland gardens or shaded foundation plantings where larger azaleas would not fit. Its early, fragrant flowers are an important nectar source for queen bumblebees and other early-emerging pollinators. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow, fibrous root system.

common_name: Candy Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Very Fragrant Pink-and-Yellow Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Candy Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred for exceptional cold hardiness, bears the most fragrant flowers of the series in soft pink streaked with pale yellow.

directions: Candy Lights, one of the most recent additions to the University of Minnesota's Northern Lights azalea series, produces exceptionally fragrant flowers in soft light pink streaked with pale yellow, opening in mid-spring on a rounded shrub reaching 5 to 6 feet. Its fragrance is noted as the strongest of the entire cold-hardy series, filling a woodland garden or shaded border with sweet perfume during its bloom window, and its nectar-rich flowers draw early bumblebees and other native pollinators. Like its sibling selections, it was bred specifically for flower-bud hardiness at the extreme cold end of the azalea's range, reliably blooming after winters that would damage less hardy deciduous azalea hybrids. Site in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells in the first two years of establishment.
